images.alt: Line drawing of four logs seen end-on, bound by one cane passing over and under the outer logs and a second cane frapped between each pair
images.caption: Roth's figure 2: how the Tully River log raft is tied. One cane (a–b) runs over the top and under the bottom of the outside logs; a second (c–d) is passed between the logs in a frapping turn, pulling the two runs together at each gap (m, n, o).
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 2

images.alt: A raft of many light saplings tied together, with a bundle of dried grass on it, on a beach by calm water
images.caption: A V-shaped raft of light saplings with its seat of dried grass, on the Wellesley Islands in the Gulf: not a Kuku Yalanji craft, but the clearest old photograph of how little a raft needs to be.
images.credit: Photograph: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), Plate II fig. 2
